It will also result in the loss of planning fees and would put pressure on the Council's revenue budget.

findings.headline: Council Tax increase held below maximum; each 1% foregone costs £250k annually
findings.detail: The council is increasing council tax by 1.99% instead of the maximum 3%. The report notes: 'The financial impact each year of not increasing Council Tax at all is an additional pressure of around £250k, assuming a 2.99% rise is foregone. Over the five-year Medium Term Financial Strategy period this would result in a loss of income of £1,250k.'
findings.matters: This is a policy choice to absorb £250k of pressure. It signals either political constraint or that the council judges resident affordability is insufficient to justify the maximum. Either way, it constrains budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Annual cost per 1% foregone: £250k; 5-year cost if maximum rise not taken: £1,250k; Increase chosen: 1.99%; Maximum allowed: 3%
findings.quote: The financial impact each year of not increasing Council Tax at all is an additional pressure of around £250k, assuming a 2.99% rise is foregone.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income collapsing; council suffering cash flow pressure from internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council is reducing its treasury investment income budget by £400k. The report states this is 'in part due to the Council having reduced levels of surplus cash due to internally borrowing' (using its own cash to fund capital rather than external borrowing).
findings.matters: This signals the council has exhausted its cash reserves and is now using operational cash flow to fund capital, leaving nothing for treasury returns. It indicates external borrowing capacity may be approaching limits.
findings.figures: Treasury investment income budget reduction: £400k
findings.quote: Income from treasury investments is below budget. This is in part due to the falling Bank of England base rate and also in part due to the Council having reduced levels of surplus cash due to internally borrowing.

findings.headline: Business rates collection fund deficit of £148k requires reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The calculation produced an overall NNDR deficit of £370k, of which Burnley's share is £148k. 'The deficit will be met from the Collection Fund Deficit Reserve.'
findings.matters: This is an immediate call on reserves for a one-off timing/collection issue. With reserves already under pressure, any repeat of collection shortfalls creates compounding stress.
findings.figures: NNDR collection fund deficit (council share): £148k
findings.quote: This year's calculation has produced an overall deficit figure of £370k of which this Council's share is £148k. The deficit will be met from the Collection Fund Deficit Reserve.

findings.headline: 2026/27 savings of £891k dependent on non-recurring pension fund revaluation
findings.detail: The £891m of additional savings required to balance the budget has been 'met by an increase in distributed pension fund surplus following the 2026/27 triennial revaluation'. This is a one-off, non-recurring item not backed by operational savings.
findings.matters: The council has not identified underlying operational savings to cover the entire pressure. Relying on pension revaluations masks the true baseline deficit and means the following year will need to identify real savings.
findings.figures: Additional savings required: £0.891m; Funded by: pension fund revaluation surplus increase
findings.quote: The additional savings required is £0.891m, which has been met by an increase in distributed pension fund surplus following the 2026/27 triennial revaluation.

findings.headline: Strategic reserves forecast to collapse 91% over five years; savings becoming riskier
findings.detail: Strategic earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £6,414k at 1 April 2025 to £561k by 31 March 2031. The council explicitly flags that 'it has become increasingly challenging to produce savings annually as the authority contracts in resource and size. Savings proposals will carry more risk of successful implementation.'
findings.matters: Depleting reserves is a classic stress signal. When combined with increasing savings risk, it indicates the council has limited flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures. The forecast assumes successful delivery of planned savings.
findings.figures: Balance as at 1/04/25: £6,414k; Balance remaining as at 31/03/2030 (forecast): £561k; Decline: 91%
findings.quote: As the authority adjusts to meet the pressures of reductions in Government funding, it has become increasingly challenging to produce savings annually as the authority contracts in resource and size. Savings proposals will carry more risk of successful implementation.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant now volume-based and uncertain; received £684k in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council received £684k for Extended Producer Responsibility in 2025/26 as part of core funding. From 2026/27 onwards the grant will be 'based on volumes collected', creating 'uncertainty around funding levels in future years'.
findings.matters: A material grant (£684k) has moved from certain to variable. If volumes collected are lower than assumed, the budget faces pressure with no planned contingency.
findings.figures: 2025/26 received: £684k; 2026/27 onwards: volume-based (amount not specified)
findings.quote: For 2026/27 onwards this grant will be based volumes collected. This results in some uncertainty around funding levels in future years.

findings.headline: Food waste statutory obligation unfunded; government settled amount not separately identified
findings.detail: From April 2026 the council must provide food waste collection. The Fair Funding Assessment includes new burdens funding but 'the amount of grant awarded has not been identified separately'. The council must find the full £650k cost 'on top of the reduction in Central Government funding'.
findings.matters: This is a statutory cost imposed by government with no dedicated funding, forcing it into the budget as a baseline pressure. It reduces flexibility to manage other budget risks.
findings.figures: £650k annual cost for food waste contract from April 2026
findings.quote: This effectively means that the Council will have to find the £650k cost of providing this service on top of the reduction in Central Government funding.

findings.headline: Business rates settlement deteriorated; council dependent on single £352k grant to balance budget
findings.detail: Burnley's business rates baseline funding decreased by £81k for 2026/27. The council's Lancashire Business Rate Pool was dissolved because the reset meant pooling no longer delivered benefits. Most critically, paragraph 26 states that a single sustainable energy grant of £352k 'plays a significant part in balancing the 2026/27 revenue budget'.
findings.matters: Budget dependency on a single, non-recurring grant is a material credit risk. Loss of that grant would immediately create a funding gap with no planned mitigation other than reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Baseline funding decrease: £81k; Sustainable energy grant: £352k; Overall business rates funding: £4.584m
findings.quote: This grant plays a significant part in balancing the 2026/27 revenue budget.

findings.headline: £36m commercial debt threatens financial viability
findings.detail: Burnley has committed circa £36m of borrowing across Pioneer Place and Charter Walk developments over 50 and 30 year terms. The council explicitly states this 'presents a threat to the financial viability of the Council', though notes it has put mitigation strategies in place including building reserves and restricting other capital schemes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's largest revenue commitments and how they interact with budget pressures. The scale of debt relative to total spending (£22.4m) and the council's declining reserves means any revenue shortfall could trigger a covenant breach.
findings.figures: £36m borrowing (circa); 50-year and 30-year terms; Pioneer Place expected to generate £0.05m surplus in 2025/26; Charter Walk expected to generate £0.2m surplus in 2025/26
findings.quote: This presents a threat to the financial viability of the Council. However, in partial mitigation, various strategies have been put in place.

findings.headline: Interest and dividend income tracking below annual budget; property fund loss exacerbates revenue shortfall.
findings.detail: Annual budget for interest and dividend income is £875k; actual interest received to Q3 is £331k (excluding dividends due), tracking 62% below budget. Property fund dividend income down from £21,993 (Q2 2024/25) to £19,361 (Q2 2025/26), and the forced redemption will reduce full-year dividend income further, creating unbudgeted revenue pressure.
findings.matters: Investment income shortfall narrows revenue budget headroom; forces council to either reduce reserves or find offsetting savings; signals investment strategy is not delivering projected returns.
findings.figures: Annual budget £875k; actual Q3 £331k; property fund dividend £19,361 (Q2 2025/26) vs £21,993 (Q2 2024/25)
findings.quote: Dividend income for the year will subsequently be below budget, and this is considered within the Treasury Management outturn forecast included in the Q3 Revenue Monitoring report elsewhere on the agenda.

findings.headline: Under-borrowed position with external borrowing timing uncertain in falling rate environment.
findings.detail: Council explicitly flags 'under-borrowed position' as a key consideration for timing external borrowing. Bank Rate cut to 3.75% with MUFG forecasting further falls, but longer-dated gilt yields remain elevated at 4.5% with uncertainty dependent on gilt issuance and political factors. Council currently relies on internal borrowing (cash balances) rather than locking in long-term debt.
findings.matters: Under-borrowed councils face refinancing risk and interest rate timing risk; delayed borrowing could result in higher costs or market access constraints; signals cash buffers under pressure.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% (cut from 4.00%); 10-year gilt yield 4.5%; average daily investment balance £7.6m
findings.quote: For the Council, given the under-borrowed position, these remain key considerations for the timing of any short or longer dated external borrowing.

findings.headline: Forced redemption of property fund with £154k capital loss realized mid-year.
findings.detail: One of two property funds (£1m original investment in 2018/19) was involuntarily redeemed when the fund merged and closed to non-Pension institutions. Council received £846k, realizing a £154k loss. While cumulative dividend income of £198k exceeded the loss by £44k, the forced redemption eliminates capital appreciation potential and reduces income diversification.
findings.matters: Forced loss signals illiquidity risk in property holdings; counterparty risk materialized; reduces financial flexibility and long-term income resilience.
findings.figures: £1m invested, £846k redeemed (£154k loss); cumulative dividends £198k exceeded loss by £44k
findings.quote: During the period, the Council was forced to 'involuntarily' redeem its interest in one of the funds, following the fund's decision to merge with a 'larger and more stable' fund, given a high volume of redemption requests from clients that risked devaluing the fund for remaining unit holders.

findings.headline: Borrowing need for capital programme increased 14% from £4.4m to £5.0m between original and revised budget.
findings.detail: Capital funding gap has widened from £4,415k (original) to £5,041k (revised), an increase of £626k. This reflects capital slippage and budget adjustments that are not fully covered by capital receipts (£1.755m), capital grants (£9.142m), or revenue funding (£5.112m).
findings.matters: Growing unfinanced capital gap means the council will need to raise more external debt; signals capital programme scale may exceed sustainable financing.
findings.figures: Borrowing need original £4,415k, revised £5,041k (£626k or 14.2% increase)
findings.quote: The net increase is due to a combination of Capital slippage brought forward from 2024/25, separate decisions approved by Members and in year budget monitoring adjustments.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement revised upward to £84.2m at Q3, up from original budget of £82.9m.
findings.detail: The CFR has been revised twice in-year: first to £83.777m at mid-year, then to £84.198m at Q3. The increases reflect capital slippage brought forward from 2024/25 and in-year capital investment approvals by Members. The trajectory shows capital plans are expanding beyond original estimates.
findings.matters: Growing capital financing requirements signal higher future debt servicing costs and capital intensity; indicates capital planning may lack contingency or faces mid-year pressures.
findings.figures: Original £82.871m → Mid-year £83.777m → Q3 £84.198m (total increase £1.327m from original)
findings.quote: At Q3, based on approved capital slippage from 2024/25, in year capital budget adjustments, including separate Capital investment decisions approved by Members, this is now estimated at £84.198m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Report (Capital Strategy 2026 to 2031)- App 4
findings.headline: Essential building maintenance backlog identified following property services insourcing and stock condition survey
findings.detail: After bringing property services back in-house, a comprehensive stock condition survey revealed essential building infrastructure works needed across council assets. The focus is on health and safety issues (staff welfare facilities, lift accessibility, mechanical and electrical safety). These are now captured in the capital programme.
findings.matters: Health and safety maintenance is a mandatory liability; the existence of a substantial backlog suggests the council had insufficient asset management oversight previously and now faces capital pressure to address these issues.
findings.figures: Budget allocation described as covering 'larger scale works' but no total value specified
findings.quote: Following the in-sourcing of the Property Services Team, a comprehensive stock condition survey was undertaken. This budget allocation covers larger scale works arising out of those building condition surveys with particular focus on staff welfare facilities (health and safety) and improved lift accessibility within Council owned assets (mechanical and electrical assessment).

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Report (Capital Strategy 2026 to 2031)- App 4
findings.headline: Staffing changes have created knowledge and skills gaps in capital management that require urgent review
findings.detail: The council has experienced significant staffing changes and personnel turnover. It now plans to conduct a review of whether the people managing capital activities have the skills and knowledge needed for the role. This suggests governance and control weaknesses in a high-value, high-risk area.
findings.matters: Skills and knowledge gaps in capital management increase risk of project delays, cost overruns, and poor financial discipline. Staffing instability in finance functions is a red flag for lenders.
findings.figures: No quantification of staffing gaps or remediation costs provided
findings.quote: In the recent past staffing levels and personnel have changed significantly. It is the Council's intention to carry out a review of the knowledge and skills of all involved in capital activities to ensure they are commensurate with the task.

findings.paper_title: Capital Budget Report (Capital Strategy 2026 to 2031)- App 4
findings.headline: Capital receipts projected to diminish, requiring sourcing of additional funding or reduction in project scope
findings.detail: The council anticipates that available capital receipts will reduce over the life of the five-year capital programme (2026-2031). This will force difficult choices between sourcing new funding, narrowing priorities, or descoping planned works. This is a structural constraint on the council's borrowing and investment capacity.
findings.matters: Declining capital receipts directly limit borrowing capacity and force descoping of schemes, affecting the council's investment plans and flexibility in response to service demands.
findings.figures: Capital receipts described as diminishing over 2026-2031 period; no quantum specified
findings.quote: Available resources are projected to diminish over the life of the capital programme due to a projected reduction in available receipt. This will have to be managed through a combination of sourcing additional funding, prioritisation of capital projects and reduction in the scope of works where possible.

findings.headline: Nearly half (49%) of five-year capital programme depends on external funding
findings.detail: £32.9m of the £67.7m five-year capital investment programme (2026-31) relies on external funding sources. This creates dependency on sources outside the council's control and introduces delivery risk if funding is delayed or withdrawn.
findings.matters: High dependency on external funding reduces predictability and council control over capital delivery; a lender would want to know which schemes rely on secured vs. uncertain external sources
findings.quote: of the £67,713,560 within the proposed CIP 2026-31, external funding totalling £32,948,302 (49%) is to be used as financing of the schemes.

findings.headline: £8.4m prudential borrowing requirement for 2026/27, with only £100k for new schemes
findings.detail: Of the £8.4m borrowing, £100k is for new investment; the remainder (£8.3m) finances existing schemes, suggesting ongoing commitments and revenue cost obligations for borrowing repayment and interest.
findings.matters: Substantial annual borrowing indicates capital pressures and recurring revenue costs; a lender would assess whether the MTFS can sustain these costs
findings.figures: £8.4m prudential borrowing; £100k new scheme
findings.quote: Of the proposed £8.4m prudential borrowing requirement for 2026/27, there is one new scheme in the sum of £100k. Provision for the repayment of principal (MRP) and interest costs are included within the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Revenue budget depends on capitalised staff recharges to capital projects
findings.detail: The paper states capitalised salaries are 'a major element' in balancing the revenue budget. Expected recharge income is £409k in 2025/26 and £400k for 2026/27. Risk: if capital projects slip, revenue loses this income source and faces a shortfall.
findings.matters: This revenue structure is fragile—a finance director and lender would be concerned about a council using capital project staffing recharges as a core revenue balancing mechanism
findings.quote: Members will be already aware that capitalised salaries are a major element in balancing the Council's revenue budget. The expected revenue income for staff time recharged against identified capital projects is £409k in 2025/26, and £400k for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast to eliminate by 31 March 2031
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that general capital receipts will reduce to zero by end of the planning period due to reduced property disposal opportunities as the council's estate reduces. This directly constrains the future capital programme.
findings.matters: Declining asset receipts reduce financial flexibility and future borrowing capacity; a lender would need to know the council's asset disposal pipeline is ending
findings.figures: General capital receipts reduce by 31 March 2031; only £642,581 of the £24.3m 2026/27 budget is financed from capital receipts
findings.quote: forecast general capital receipts reduce by 31 March 2031. This is due to reduced opportunities to realise capital receipts, as the estate reduces, which will leave a lesser capital programme going forward.

findings.headline: Pension contribution cost fell substantially due to fund surplus, providing a one-off relief, but fund is volatile.
findings.detail: The employer pension contribution rate decreased from 19.4% to 16.5% for 2026/27-2028/29 following the 2025 revaluation. This is positive. However, the council notes it is 'particularly sensitive to volatility of returns due to the value of its assets and liabilities in the fund in comparison to the value of Burnley's current contributors to the fund (current payroll), which is 16 times smaller than its liabilities'. Burnley has a 16:1 liability-to-payroll ratio compared to larger councils' lower ratios.
findings.matters: While the contribution rate drop is a genuine saving, the council's high liability-to-payroll ratio makes it vulnerable to further volatility swings, which could reverse the gain or require higher contributions at the 2028 revaluation.
findings.figures: Contribution rate: 19.4% (2022-2025) → 16.5% (2026-2029). Fund liability-to-payroll ratio: 16:1 for Burnley.
findings.quote: Burnley is particularly sensitive to volatility of returns due to the value of its assets and liabilities in the fund in comparison to the value of Burnley's current contributors to the fund (current payroll), which is 16 times smaller than its liabilities.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty may force further strategy revision within the MTFS period.
findings.detail: The council submitted a 5-model LGR proposal by 28 November 2025, with central government expected to decide before Parliamentary summer recess 2026. If approved, Burnley would be merged into a new unitary authority, fundamentally changing the council's structure and financial baseline. The MTFS acknowledges LGR 'has the potential to significantly impact on the development of the Council's Financial Strategy'.
findings.matters: A lender has no certainty whether this council will exist in its current form from 2027 onwards. LGR could alter the financial position (through merger of services, assets, or liabilities) and could require one-off transformation costs.
findings.figures: LGR decision expected before summer 2026 recess. 5-model approach submitted by Burnley proposing 5 new unitary authorities in Lancashire.
findings.quote: On the basis of current timelines, proposals for LGR were submitted to Government by 28th November 2025 with the Government deciding on LGR in Lancashire before the Parliamentary Summer recess in 2026.

findings.headline: Strategic earmarked reserves are forecast to decline to minimum levels by the end of the MTFS period, limiting headroom for shocks.
findings.detail: The reserves forecast shows strategic earmarked reserves falling from £6.414m (1 April 2025) to £3.256m by 31 March 2030, a decline of 49%. The council notes 'a substantial part of the Council's strategic earmarked reserves will be around their recommended minimum level by the end of the MTFS period'. This leaves little buffer for emerging risks or delivery failures.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves over the MTFS period means the council will have less ability to absorb a funding shock or savings shortfall in the later years of the forecast period.
findings.figures: Strategic earmarked reserves: 1 April 2025 £6,414k → 31 March 2030 £3,256k. Decline of £3,158k (49%).
findings.quote: It can be seen in the table above however that it is anticipated that a substantial part of the Council's strategic earmarked reserves will be around their recommended minimum level by the end of the MTFS period.

findings.headline: Retail, Hospitality and Leisure rate relief removal and revaluation may worsen business rates collection.
findings.detail: The council's previous RHL relief of 40% (capped at £105k per business) is being removed and replaced with multipliers 5p below standard rates for properties below £500k. A business property revaluation took effect 1 April 2026 with large increases in some rateable values. The council explicitly flags that these changes 'may impact on collection rates for 2026/27 onwards'.
findings.matters: The less generous relief replacement combined with the revaluation creates risk that business rates collection falls below the budgeted baseline, eroding a key income source at a time of funding stress.
findings.figures: Previous RHL relief was 40% capped at £105k. New multiplier is 5p below standard (not capped). Revaluation based on property values at 1 April 2024.
findings.quote: This will be replaced by new business rate multipliers which will set multipliers at 5p below the relevant national multipliers for RHL properties with a rateable value below £500k. This may impact on collection rates for 2026/27 onwards.

findings.headline: The Lancashire Business Rates Pool has been dissolved, removing a source of prior-year growth funding.
findings.detail: Burnley was a member of the 50% Lancashire pool in 2025/26. The Fair Funding Review rolled all prior year business rates growth into the general allocation, making pooling uneconomical. The pool dissolved for 2026/27. While central government provides a 100% safety net in 2026/27, this drops to 92.5% from 2027/28, creating exposure to business rates shortfalls.
findings.matters: The council loses the inflation-protected element of business rates pooling and faces direct exposure to collection volatility from 2027/28 onwards, at a time when RHL relief changes may impact collection rates.
findings.figures: 100% safety net 2026/27 only. Safety net drops to 92.5% from 2027/28.
findings.quote: As a result, the Lancashire Business Rates Pool has been dissolved for 2026/27 but will be reviewed for future years.

findings.headline: The council forecasts a cumulative budget gap of £1.7m over 2027/30 that will need to be closed by savings or reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies funding gaps of £0.3m (2027/28), £0.5m (2028/29), and £0.9m (2029/30), totalling £1.7m over the three-year period. These gaps assume pay awards of 3% and fee/charge income growth of 2%, but are not dependent on reserves being used as the primary balancing mechanism. The council notes the cumulative gap is 7.6%.
findings.matters: The council will need to find recurring savings totalling £1.7m or face drawing strategic reserves. Combined with the food waste burden and funding cuts, this signals sustained pressure on service delivery.
findings.quote: Cumulative Potential Gap 2027/30 1.7 7.6

findings.headline: A £650k unfunded Food Waste implementation burden arrives in April 2026 on top of the funding cut.
findings.detail: The council was promised new burdens funding for Food Waste implementation from DEFRA, but central government rolled the cost into the Fair Funding Allocation rather than providing additional grant. The council must find £650k in 2026/27 to implement a statutory service that was supposed to be funded separately.
findings.matters: This is a demand the council cannot refuse and cannot fund from existing budgets; it either cuts other services or draws on reserves at the start of the MTFS period.
findings.figures: £650k cost in 2026/27 for Food Waste provision.
findings.quote: This means that the Council will have to find the estimated £650k cost of providing this service in 2026/27 in addition to the reduction in Central Government funding.

findings.headline: Burnley is far more dependent on central government grants than other councils, making it uniquely exposed to funding volatility.
findings.detail: In 2026/27, 31% of Burnley's spending power comes from Revenue Support Grant compared to 19% for England's average council. This rises from 13% in 2025/26. By contrast, other councils average just 2-3% RSG dependency historically. This structural vulnerability means Burnley cannot absorb funding cuts through buoyancy in council tax or business rates as other councils can.
findings.matters: A lender assessing Burnley's financial resilience must see that the council cannot buffer grant losses through local revenue growth; grant dependency leaves it entirely exposed to central policy.
findings.figures: 2026/27: Burnley 31% RSG vs England average 19%. 2025/26: Burnley 13% vs England average 3%. Historical data 2024/25: Burnley 12% vs England average 3%.
findings.quote: Whilst this would be a concern nationally, the reduction will impact Burnley greater as it is more heavily dependent on Central Government funding than other councils which have greater buoyancy in their Council Tax and Business Rates base.

findings.headline: Burnley faces a 15% reduction in central government funding over three years despite high deprivation.
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 settlement shows Burnley's funding allocation dropping from £12.987m (adjusted 2025/26) to £10.028m by 2028/29, a cumulative 15.06% reduction. This reduction is front-loaded, with 6.58% cut in 2026/27 alone. The council explicitly notes the reduction is substantial despite the council having high levels of deprivation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of the council's funding cliff and whether cost reductions can keep pace with grant cuts.
findings.quote: This shows a substantial reduction in Central Government funding through the Fair Funding Review for the Council, despite the Council having high levels of deprivation.

findings.headline: Waste contract vehicle procurement needs to be accelerated to meet critical April 2026 deadline
findings.detail: £1.568m in waste collection vehicles must be reverse-slipped from 2026/27 into 2025/26 to ensure fleet availability when the new waste contract begins on 1 April 2026. This is a service-critical timing constraint that leaves no margin for delivery delays.
findings.matters: A failure to deliver vehicles on time would disrupt waste collection services across the borough and expose the council to contract performance penalties.
findings.figures: £1.568m; contract commencement 1 April 2026
findings.quote: As noted at Q2, to ensure available fleet for contract commencement from 1 April 2026, will require 'reverse slippage' from 2026/27 in the sum of £1.568m to ensure timely delivery.

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing increased by £627k and locked in additional debt service
findings.detail: Q3 monitoring has increased the planned borrowing requirement from the original £4,414,266 to £5,041,430. This additional £627k in borrowing creates permanent revenue consequences: £25k extra annual MRP (principal repayment) and £151k in interest costs annually at 3% interest, both now baked into future budgets.
findings.matters: Growing debt service costs constrain revenue spending flexibility, especially important if the council faces unexpected income pressure or demand shocks.
findings.figures: £627k additional borrowing; £25k additional MRP; £151k annual interest at 3%
findings.quote: The revenue implications of borrowing an additional £627k at Q3 are an increase over the current Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) budget included within the MTFS of £25k and an interest charge, assuming 3% on the total borrowing of £5,041,430 at Q3, of £151k for a full year.

findings.headline: Future capital financing depends on selling properties marked as high risk
findings.detail: The council's capital investment programme requires asset sales over the medium term. Some of these property disposals are explicitly flagged as high-risk, and the report warns that if receipts are not received, alternative financing will be needed—meaning additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if the council's funding strategy depends on uncertain asset sales, especially ones the council itself considers risky. Property market volatility could force additional debt.
findings.figures: Properties to be sold over medium-term CIP; some are high risk
findings.quote: Please note, the general receipts position requires a number of properties to be sold over the life of the medium-term Capital Investment Programme (CIP), some of which are considered high risk. ... Should these receipts not be received, we will need to source alternative financing.

findings.headline: Capital resources base is shrinking and constraining future investment
findings.detail: The council's available capital receipts are declining because property sales opportunities are reducing as the estate shrinks. The report states this will require prioritisation of future capital schemes in line with falling resources. The forecast surplus at 31 March 2026 is £2,484,151, but the underlying trend is downward.
findings.matters: A contracting capital funding base limits the council's ability to invest in infrastructure and modernisation, and could constrain its ability to fund borrowing repayment if revenue deteriorates.
findings.figures: Forecast surplus of £2,484,151 at 31 March 2026; resources reducing each financial year
findings.quote: The resources are reducing each financial year. This is due to reduced opportunities to realise capital receipts, as the estate reduces, which will require prioritisation of future capital schemes in line with available resources.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation on the horizon creates material uncertainty for the council's going concern status.
findings.detail: The council identifies Local Government Reorganisation as a factor that must be managed alongside the budget gap. The strategy explicitly addresses the need to maintain financial viability as a going concern despite this pending organisational change.
findings.matters: Reorganisation could fundamentally change asset holdings, borrowing capacity, service scope, and staffing; it introduces an existential risk alongside the financial gap.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: the need for consideration of the medium term financial position is paramount to ensuring sustainable service delivery and for the Council to remain viable as a going concern, even with Local Government Reorganisation on the horizon.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review outcome has reduced government funding, the primary driver of the budget gap.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the outcome of the Fair Funding Review has reduced government funding, combined with pressures on other income. This is the root cause of the £1.7m gap. Government funding is typically a council's largest single revenue source.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the gap stems from reduced government funding rather than local overspending; this affects assessments of financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £1.7m gap attributed to government funding reduction and other income pressures
findings.quote: Given the reduction in Government funding, pressures on other income and expenditure in addition to Local Government Reorganisation, the Council endeavours to meet those financial challenges taking a strategic view whilst protecting the quality of services and minimising the impact on residents.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £1.7m over 2027/28-2030/31, representing 9.1% of current net budget.
findings.detail: The council must close a £1.7m budget gap across four years starting in 2027/28. This is a material proportion of the 2025/26 net budget of £18.721m and represents the fundamental financial challenge driving the strategy, requiring either significant spending reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can deliver multi-year savings programmes without service deterioration or unsustainable reserve depletion; this figure is the baseline for that assessment.
findings.figures: £1.7m cumulative gap; 9.1% of 2025/26 net budget of £18.721m
findings.quote: The headline reduction, over the four financial years 2027/28, 2028/29, 2029/30 and 2030/31 is a cumulative budget gap of £1.7m (9.1% of the 2025/26 net budget of £18.721m).

findings.headline: Council deliberately underborrowed but explicitly signals future borrowing requirement for capital programme
findings.detail: Current external debt (£56m at March 2026) is substantially below the Capital Financing Requirement (£81-92m). This underborrowed position is deliberate while interest rates are elevated, but the council directly acknowledges this creates a future borrowing obligation.
findings.matters: The gap between current debt and CFR represents deferred borrowing that will be required when capital needs escalate or rates fall; lenders must factor in this future financing obligation to credit risk.
findings.figures: External debt at 31 March 2026: £56m. CFR 2026/27: £90.4m. Under Liability Benchmark 2026/27: £26.3m
findings.quote: This means that the council is maintaining an underborrowed position, which is prudent whilst interest rates for borrowing are high, but also indicates that future borrowing may be required in order to fund the council's capital programme or to repay debt.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing to £90.4m by 2026/27, requiring increasing net borrowing
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow from £84.2m in 2025/26 to £90.4m in 2026/27. After capital receipts, grants and revenue contributions, the net borrowing need in 2026/27 is £8.4m, up from £5.0m the previous year.
findings.matters: A growing CFR and increasing net borrowing requirement signal escalating capital financing obligations that will determine the council's long-term debt burden and financial sustainability.
findings.quote: Any capital expenditure above, which has not immediately been paid for, will increase the CFR and is represented by the net financing need for the year line.

findings.headline: Financing costs consuming a rising share of revenue budget, driven by government grant reductions and higher borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council forecasts that the cost of servicing debt will take up a growing proportion of its net revenue stream. This trend reflects both declining government funding and higher interest rates on borrowing for the capital programme.
findings.matters: Rising financing cost burden constrains the revenue budget available for service delivery and indicates deteriorating affordability of capital investment.
findings.figures: No specific percentage change disclosed; the council notes the Final Local Government Finance Settlement was awaited at time of writing.
findings.quote: This is due to forecast reductions in future aggregate external funding based on 'revenue spending power' for the Council through reduced Government grant, together with increased borrowing costs to fund the council's capital programme.

findings.headline: Capital programme nearly halves over three years, falling 77% by 2027/28
findings.detail: Capital expenditure programmed at £24.123m for 2025/26 falls to £11.927m in 2026/27 and £5.562m in 2027/28, a sharp decline. This follows actual spend of £32.260m in 2023/24 and £22.236m in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A sustained decline in capital investment of this magnitude indicates either financial constraint on the council's ability to sustain capital spending or reassessment of service priorities, both material to lenders

findings.detail: The Authorised Limit for external debt increased from £100.274m to £107.012m for 2025/26, with operational boundary rising from £91.158m to £97.284m. This revision suggests borrowing needs have been reassessed upward since the original March 2025 approval.
findings.matters: Mid-year increases to borrowing authority indicate either capital plans have changed or debt servicing costs have increased, material to understanding the council's financial trajectory

findings.headline: Prudential borrowing increased by £157k at Q2, adding £44k annual MRP cost and £137k annual interest charge.
findings.detail: Revised capital programme increases planned borrowing from £4.41m to £4.57m. This £157k additional borrowing adds £44k to annual Minimum Revenue Provision (capital repayment charge) and £137k annual interest costs at assumed 3%. These costs persist across the life of the assets, reducing revenue flexibility.
findings.matters: Increasing borrowing adds to debt burden and recurring revenue costs. Over a medium-term capital plan, these carry-forward charges accumulate and constrain the council's ability to respond to future pressures or invest in other priorities.
findings.figures: £157k additional borrowing; total planned borrowing £4,571,055; £44k additional annual MRP; £137k annual interest (at 3%)
findings.quote: The revised Capital Programme for 2025/26, including proposed budget adjustments now estimates the planned borrowing requirement for the year to be £4,571,055. The revenue implications of borrowing an additional £157k at Q2 are an increase over the current Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) budget included within the MTFS of £44k and an interest charge, assuming 3% on the total borrowing of £4,571,055 at Q2, of £137k for a full year.

findings.headline: Major capital commitments (Waste Transfer Station, Heritage regeneration) approved without finalised budgets; implementation and financing deferred to 2026-31.
findings.detail: Council approved on 8 October 2025 a Waste Strategy requiring capital investment in a Waste Transfer Station, depot relocation, and new contract vehicles, plus a High 5 4 Heritage five-year civic regeneration programme. Both are committed to start 2026/27 but detailed budgets and financing are not yet determined. These programmes 'will form part of the developing Capital Investment Programme (CIP) 2026-31' with 'an estimated spend profile' to be included later. This creates forward capital pressure and likely additional borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A lender needs forward visibility of committed capital programmes and borrowing needs. Major programmes approved without finalised budgets or funding plans signal capital pressure and increase uncertainty around future debt levels.
findings.figures: Five-year heritage programme starting 2026/27; waste programme starting 2026/27; specific costs not yet determined
findings.quote: The approved budget will form part of the developing Capital Investment Programme (CIP) 2026-31 with costs likely to fall in 2026/27. The CIP will be considered as part of Budget Council in March 26 with any re-profiling requirements ie earlier spend within 2025/26 reported through these regular Capital monitoring updates.

findings.headline: Council's capital financing model relies on declining asset sales, with some properties identified as high-risk.
findings.detail: Capital receipts are falling each year as the council's property estate shrinks. The report explicitly identifies that properties required to be sold over the medium-term capital plan include some 'considered high risk', and warns that if these sales do not materialize, 'we will need to source alternative financing'. Forecast surplus capital receipts at 31 March 2026 are £1,898,701. This signals increasing reliance on borrowing as the real estate base erodes.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can finance its approved capital programme without forced borrowing. Declining asset base combined with concentration on high-risk disposals suggests potential future cash constraints and increasing leverage.
findings.figures: £1,898,701 forecast balance at 31 March 2026; receipts declining year-on-year due to 'reduced opportunities' as estate reduces
findings.quote: The resources are reducing each financial year. This is due to reduced opportunities to realise capital receipts, as the estate reduces, which will require prioritisation of future capital schemes in line with available resources. Please note, the general receipts position requires a number of properties to be sold over the life of the medium-term Capital Investment Programme (CIP), some of which are considered high risk. Should these receipts not be received, we will need to source alternative financing.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges that future borrowing is necessary despite currently under-borrowed position
findings.detail: The council maintains an under-borrowed position using reserves and balances rather than external debt, but explicitly states this 'indicates that future borrowing may be required in order to fund the council's capital programme or to repay debt.' This signals reserves are not a sustainable long-term capital funding source.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite; acknowledging they cannot fund ongoing capital needs signals the council will move from its current under-borrowed position to active debt issuance, increasing reliance on debt markets.
findings.figures: External debt £60m; Capital Financing Requirement £83.777m (2025/26); underborrowed position £20.279m (2025/26)
findings.quote: This means that the council is maintaining an underborrowed position, which is prudent whilst interest rates for borrowing are high, but also indicates that future borrowing may be required in order to fund the council's capital programme or to repay debt.

findings.headline: Capital programme projected to fall 77% from 2025/26 to 2027/28
findings.detail: Programmed capital expenditure is forecast to decline sharply from £24.1m in 2025/26 to £11.9m in 2026/27 and £5.6m in 2027/28. This steep contraction suggests either major capital schemes completing or capital investment rationing due to affordability constraints.
findings.matters: Sharp capital spending cuts signal either deferred maintenance building up or capital rationing due to financing pressures, both of which affect the council's service sustainability and long-term asset condition.

This £6m upward revision in three months signals either accelerated borrowing drawdown, higher-than-forecast cash outflows, or revised funding assumptions.
findings.matters: Unexpectedly higher debt in the short term and frequent forecast revisions suggest cash flow is tighter than anticipated, which affects refinancing risk and debt servicing capacity.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley audit finds good controls but minor weaknesses in 2025/26
news_drafts.lead: Burnley council's internal audit for 2025/26 found that the authority has a good system of controls but minor weaknesses in design or consistency of application may put achievement of some objectives at risk. The council met 100% of its high-priority audit actions against its target. An audit review of the council's acquisition of the Charter Walk shopping centre found risks were identified, controlled and continue to be monitored, receiving comprehensive assurance. The council's chief internal auditor lacks required professional qualifications, which the council is working to address. Some lower-priority audit recommendations have been delayed in implementation.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley council draws down reserves at sharp pace as unidentified savings threaten budget
news_drafts.lead: Burnley council drew £4.979m from its reserves in the first quarter of 2026/27, reducing its earmarked reserves from £24.339m to £19.360m in three months. The council is drawing on its money set aside for known future needs because it is funding capital schemes—buildings, roads and equipment—through internal borrowing, using its own cash instead of taking bank loans to save on interest. However, the papers show this approach's sustainability "remains under continual review". At the same time, the council has identified only £83k of the £259k in budgeted savings it committed to deliver this year, leaving £176k unaccounted for. The council's own papers state that current economic pressures "may threaten the achievement of these targets". If those savings are not found, the council's forecast break-even position will not materialise, and reserves will deplete faster still.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley Council faces £1.7m three-year budget gap with no savings plan to close it
news_drafts.lead: Burnley Council is forecasting a £215k overspend in the current financial year, a reversal from a budgeted surplus of £39k, because it has failed to identify £176k of planned savings in the first quarter. The council budgeted £259k in cost reductions for 2026/27 but has found only £83k so far. Looking ahead, its medium-term financial plan shows budget gaps totalling £1.842m over the next three years, with approved savings of just £160k. The remaining £1.682m shortfall has no identified proposals to close it. The forecast overspend is compounded by unresolved pay negotiations—a 1% higher pay award than budgeted would cost an additional £122k—and a £600k cut in government funding announced at the final settlement in February, which the council has temporarily offset but fears may not continue next year.
